Minor Planet Center data · 1,580,046 asteroids

Reading the Asteroid Belt

Three graphs built from the master list of every known asteroid orbit. For each one: how to read it, what stands out, and what the data does not let us claim.

Four terms first

auAstronomical unit, the average Earth to Sun distance (about 150 million km). Orbit sizes here are in au.
Semi-major axis (a)The size of an orbit. Mars is at about 1.5 au, Jupiter at 5.2 au.
Eccentricity (e)How stretched an orbit is. 0 is a perfect circle, values near 1 are long ovals.
Near-Earth objectAn asteroid whose orbit brings it close to Earth's neighbourhood. The Minor Planet Center flags these in its file.

1. The map of every orbit

all 1,580,046   near-Earth objects, 43,052   designated in 2026, 21,101

How to read it

Left to right is orbit size in au. Bottom to top is eccentricity. A dot at the bottom is on a nearly circular path; a dot near the top swings in close to the Sun and back out far.

What to notice

Most asteroids sit in the main belt, between about 2 and 3.3 au, which is the region between Mars and Jupiter. Near-Earth objects (red) sit in the upper left because their stretched orbits reach in toward Earth. Two smaller clumps sit outside the main belt, one near 4 au and one at 5.2 au, which is Jupiter's own orbit size. We did not look into what they are.

What we can't say

Red is drawn last, so it covers other dots where they overlap. Density in the picture is therefore not a reliable count. Blue marks only a 2026 designation. It does not tell us which telescope found the asteroid.

2. The gaps in the belt

ResonanceOrbit size (au)What the data shows
4:12.06Clear gap
3:12.50Clear gap
5:22.82Clear gap
7:32.96Only a faint dip
2:13.28Clear gap; the belt ends here

How to read it

A "3:1" resonance means an asteroid circles the Sun 3 times while Jupiter circles once. Kepler's third law turns that ratio into an orbit size, a = 5.2026 au × (1/3)^(2/3) = 2.50 au. At that size Jupiter tugs the asteroid at the same point of every lap, and the repeated pushes eventually throw it onto another orbit.

What to notice

The calculated positions line up with real drops in the count. These emptied stripes are the Kirkwood gaps, and the physics explains where they fall.

What we can't say

The 7:3 line sits on a much weaker dip than the others, so it is not a clean gap. The small bump between 1.8 and 2.0 au is a separate group we have not identified. The gaps are also blurred because we used each asteroid's current orbit. Long-term average orbits would probably look sharper, though we have not tested that.

3. New asteroids over time

YearAsteroids designated
202426,246
202573,305
2026 (so far)21,108

How to read it

A name like 2025 AQ10 encodes when the asteroid was first reported. The year comes first, then a letter for the half-month (A is Jan 1–15, B is Jan 16–31, and so on). We decoded every name from 2024 to 2026 and counted them. 120,659 asteroids are in this chart.

What to notice

There is a huge spike in mid-2025, with about 17,000 new names in one half-month, many times a normal 2024 bar. After the spike, counts in 2026 are much lower.

What we can't say

The assignment suggests the spike comes from the new Rubin telescope. Nothing in this chart shows that, because a name records when an object was first seen, not who saw it. We do not know why 2026 is lower. The last bars (November 2026) are incomplete.

Open questions

  • Why did the count spike in mid-2025, and why is 2026 lower?
  • What is the group of asteroids at 1.8–2.0 au?
  • Next test: look up the observations for a sample of 2026 asteroids and count how many carry Rubin's observatory code, X05.
